plan.title: bug(merge): a PR that conflicts with its base is reported as absent-required, not as a conflict

narratives.Description: When a PR conflicts with its base branch, GitHub does not run its pull_request CI, so pr:wait-mergeable-and-merge waits, finds the required checks absent and reports absent-required, which workers read as a CI problem. This story adds one REST read of pulls/<N> after the monitor ends with absent-required or cap-reached; when GitHub reports mergeable_state dirty the verb reports the outcome base-conflict with exit 1 and an error that names the base branch and the merge-or-rebase fix. Every other case keeps today's outcome and text, and no gate, flag, exit code or stored state is added.
narratives.Overview:
1. Trigger. In `waitMergeableAndMerge`, after `classifyMonitorOutcome`, when the outcome is `absent-required` or `cap-reached`, the verb makes one REST read of `pulls/<N>`. This applies in direct mode and in merge-queue mode, because the monitor runs before the enqueue. No other outcome makes the read. A clean monitor run makes no extra call. The outcomes the verb returns before the monitor (preflight refusals, `semantic-green-blocked` and its named outcomes, `new-p0-p1`) are unchanged.
2. Reader. One new reader in `packages/core/src/pr-wait-mergeable/` takes `mergeable_state` and `base.ref` from that one response. It is injectable through one new option on `WaitMergeableOptions`. Under the existing test-harness convention (`skipHumanMergeGate` or `VITEST`, no injected function) the read is skipped, as for `watchFn` and `mergeQueueDetectFn`.
3. Conflict outcome. When `mergeable_state` is `dirty`, the verb reports the outcome `base-conflict` with exit 1 (`EXIT_TIMEOUT_OR_ESCALATION`); its error text says that PR #N conflicts with its base branch and names that branch from `base.ref` (or says "its base branch" when `base.ref` is missing), says that required checks do not run on a conflicted PR only when the replaced outcome is `absent-required`, names the fix (merge or rebase the base branch into the PR branch, resolve the conflicts, push, then run `task pr:wait-mergeable-and-merge` again), and names the replaced monitor outcome; the monitor payload stays in `monitor_result`.
4. Fallback. When the read fails, cannot be parsed, or gives any state other than `dirty` (including `unknown`, null, `blocked`, `behind` and `unstable`, whatever `mergeable` says), the verb reports today's outcome, exit code and error text unchanged.
5. Unchanged. No new exit code, flag, gate, refusal or stored state. The printed result label for exit 1 stays `TIMEOUT-OR-ESCALATION`; `outcome` and `error` carry the conflict. The merge-queue `--resume` / `--wait` path is not changed.
6. Docs. The #6467 line under "Known issues" in `content/docs/github-merge-queue-setup.md` says that on 0.129.11 a conflicted PR shows `absent-required`, and that from the release with #6467 the verb reports `base-conflict` and names the fix. The line keeps `#6467` and `absent-required`, which the `merge_queue_playbook_6366` lock test requires.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a monitor result `absent-required` and a read with `mergeable_state` `dirty` and `base.ref` `master`, when the verb runs, then the outcome is `base-conflict`, the exit code is 1, and the error names the conflict with `master`, says required checks do not run on a conflicted PR, and names the merge-or-rebase fix.
- Given a monitor result `cap-reached` and a read with `mergeable_state` `dirty`, when the verb runs, then the outcome is `base-conflict`, the exit code is 1, and the error names the conflict and the fix and does not say that required checks do not run.
- Given a monitor result `absent-required` and a read with `mergeable_state` `blocked`, when the verb runs, then the outcome is `absent-required` and the error text is the same as today.
- Given a monitor result `absent-required` and a read that fails, or gives `unknown` or null, when the verb runs, then the outcome is `absent-required` and the error text is the same as today.
- Given a read with `mergeable_state` `dirty` and no `base.ref`, when the verb reports `base-conflict`, then the error says "its base branch" and still names the fix.
- Given a clean monitor result, when the verb runs, then the conflict read is not made.
- Given a SHA-matched `new-p0-p1` probe before the monitor, when the verb runs, then the outcome is `new-p0-p1` and the conflict read is not made.
- Given merge-queue mode, a monitor result `absent-required` and a `dirty` read, when the verb runs, then the outcome is `base-conflict` and the PR is not enqueued.
- Given `--json` and a `base-conflict` result, then standard output is one JSON document with `outcome` `base-conflict` and the error text.
- `content/docs/github-merge-queue-setup.md` Known issues names `base-conflict` for #6467 and still contains `#6467` and `absent-required`.
narratives.Constraint:

## In plain English
When a PR conflicts with its base branch, GitHub does not run the PR's CI, so the required checks never appear. The merge command waits, sees the checks are missing, and reports `absent-required`. A worker reads that as a CI problem and waits or escalates, while the real fix is to merge or rebase the base branch. The recommended fix changes only the report: when the wait ends without a merge, the command reads GitHub's merge state for the PR once, and if GitHub says the PR conflicts, it reports a conflict outcome that names the fix. It adds no gate, no new exit code and no new wait. The open question for the critic is whether that one read is in the right place and covers the Acceptance Criteria.

## Pains
The pains are exactly the issue's Acceptance Criteria as written.
- P1 — Given a PR whose `mergeable_state` is `dirty`, when `pr:wait-mergeable-and-merge` runs, then it reports a conflict outcome that says the PR conflicts with its base and names the fix (merge or rebase the base branch).
- P2 — Given a PR whose `mergeable_state` is `dirty`, when its required checks are absent, then the verb does not report `absent-required`.
- P3 — Given a PR with no conflict and missing required checks, when the verb runs, then it still reports `absent-required` as today.

## Constraints (not pains)
- No new gate, refusal, grant or exit code. A conflicted PR still ends with exit 1, as `absent-required` does today.
- The merge-queue `--resume` / `--wait` path (#6423) is unchanged; the queue already names a `merge_conflict` removal.
- A failed or unclear read of the merge state never makes the result worse than today.

## Anchors at the dispatch SHA
- `packages/core/src/pr-wait-mergeable/cascade.ts` 607-628: the verb runs the monitor, maps its exit with `classifyMonitorOutcome`, and returns any non-`clean` outcome with `error: monitor exited <rc> (outcome=<outcome>)`. The enqueue (merge-queue mode) at 772-789 comes after this, so both modes pass through it.
- `packages/core/src/pr-wait-mergeable/classify.ts` 16-17 and 27-28: monitor `ABSENT-REQUIRED` or exit 4 maps to `absent-required`, exit 1. Nothing reads `mergeable_state`.
- `packages/core/src/pr-monitor/monitor.ts` 231-245: absent-required escalates from CI data only (`readAbsentRequiredContexts`); 92-114 `mergeStateFromPayload` feeds only the heartbeat line.
- `packages/core/src/pr-merge-readiness/compute.ts` 460-470: on the main path the readiness payload reads mergeability only after review and CI pass, so an absent-required payload usually has no `mergeable_state` in it.
- `packages/core/src/pr-merge-readiness/mergeability.ts` 28-66: `fetchMergeability` is an existing one-call REST read of `pulls/<N>` that returns `mergeable_state` and `mergeable`.
- `packages/core/src/pr-wait-mergeable/main.ts` 315-330: text output prints `outcome:` and `error:` lines; `--json` prints `outcome` and `error`.
- `content/docs/github-merge-queue-setup.md` 97: "Known issues" line for #6467 tells the reader to merge master and re-run.

## Recommended mechanism (the thing to critique)
- C1. After the monitor, when the outcome is `absent-required` or `cap-reached`, the verb makes one REST read of `pulls/<N>` with the existing `fetchMergeability` reader.
- C2. When that read gives `mergeable_state` `dirty`, the verb reports a new outcome `base-conflict` with exit 1 (the same code as today). The error text says the PR conflicts with its base branch, names the base branch, says that required checks do not run on a conflicted PR, and names the fix: merge or rebase the base branch into the PR branch, resolve the conflicts, push, and run the verb again.
- C3. When the read fails, or gives any other state (including `unknown` or null while GitHub is still computing), the verb reports today's outcome and text unchanged.
- C4. No other outcome changes. No new exit code, flag, gate or stored state. The read happens only on the two outcomes in C1, so a clean run makes no extra call.
- C5. Docs: the #6467 line under "Known issues" in `content/docs/github-merge-queue-setup.md` is replaced by one line that names the `base-conflict` outcome and its fix.

Questions for the critic:
1. Should `cap-reached` be in C1, or only `absent-required` as the issue names it?
2. Should the verb also read the merge state once before the monitor starts, so a PR that is already conflicted is reported at once rather than after the monitor's grace polls?
3. Is `mergeable_state` `dirty` alone the right test, or should `mergeable` `false` also count?

Worktree HEAD file is `2f30fc5a4716fe53ad7011b0ea5da22debd5145d`. The shell hook denied `git show` because `node_modules/@deftai/directive-runtime` is missing. The lines below are from that checkout.

## In plain English

When a pull request conflicts with its base, GitHub does not start the pull-request checks. The merge command waits, sees the required checks missing, and reports `absent-required`. Whoever is watching treats that as a CI problem. The fix is to merge or rebase the base branch into the pull request and run the command again.

The recommended mechanism is the right one and can bind. After the monitor, and only when that ending is `absent-required` or `cap-reached`, read the pull request once. If GitHub's merge state is `dirty`, report `base-conflict`, keep exit 1, and name the merge-or-rebase fix. A failed read, or any other state, keeps today's outcome and text. A clean run makes no extra call. The merge-queue resume and wait path stays as it is.

`cap-reached` stays in that read. A conflicted pull request whose checks failed, are still running, or were never classed as absent waits out the cap and never becomes `absent-required`. Limiting the read to `absent-required` leaves those as a timeout.

The read stays after the monitor. The command already fetches the pull request while detecting the merge queue, and that first response is often still unknown. The later read, after the one-poll grace, is the one that can see `dirty`. Returning early on the first body would miss a cold conflict.

The positive test is the state string `dirty` alone. A known state such as `blocked`, `behind`, or `unstable` keeps today's outcome, including when `mergeable` is false.

Two statement changes belong with that mechanism. The existing mergeability reader does not return the base branch, so the branch name comes from the same response. And this conflict report replaces only those two monitor endings. A review finding or a red master gate that returns earlier stays that earlier report.

## Road not taken

Returning immediately when the queue-detection fetch is already `dirty` would skip the grace. That fetch already happens (`merge-queue.ts` 117-130) and keeps only `base.ref`. The same code maps a null `mergeable` to unknown (`mergeability.ts` 9-10, 63), which is what a first fetch often is while GitHub computes the state. Branching on that body would miss the cold conflict and would still need the later read. One site, after the monitor classifies the ending, is enough. A requirement that a known-dirty pull request must not spend the grace would flip this.

## 1. The mergeability reader cannot name the base branch — sharpens-framing

Evidence: `packages/core/src/pr-merge-readiness/mergeability.ts` 14-17 and 58-65. `fetchMergeability` returns `mergeableState`, `mergeable`, and `error`. `packages/core/src/pr-wait-mergeable/merge-queue.ts` 116-130 reads `base.ref` from the same `pulls/<N>` body and drops the merge state. `cascade.ts` 530-545 stores only whether queue mode is on, so `detection.branch` is gone by the time the monitor returns.

Failure mode: a call to `fetchMergeability`, as C1 names it, can see `dirty` and still have no branch name for the C2 sentence. A second call to the base-ref reader is a second GET, and a missing name can be treated as "skip the conflict report."

Disposition consequence: the one response supplies both `mergeable_state` and `base.ref`. A missing `base.ref` still reports `base-conflict` and the merge-or-rebase fix.

## 2. The acceptance text is wider than the two endings — sharpens-framing

Evidence: `cascade.ts` 557-575 returns `semantic-green-blocked` before the monitor on the non-queue path. Queue mode skips that block (`cascade.ts` 557). `cascade.ts` 590-604 returns `new-p0-p1` before the monitor. The mechanism edits the non-clean return at `cascade.ts` 613-629, and only for `absent-required` and `cap-reached`.

Failure mode: a dirty pull request that already has a SHA-matched P0, or a non-queue pull request blocked on the master gate, still reports that earlier outcome. Calling the unconditional "whenever `dirty`" acceptance satisfied would be a false relief. Folding those returns into `base-conflict` would hide the P0 or the red gate.

Disposition consequence: relief of that acceptance is the two monitor endings only. The earlier returns stay as they are, and the bound says so.

## 3. The checks sentence is wrong for a cap ending — sharpens-framing

Evidence: `packages/core/src/pr-monitor/absent-required.ts` 35-48. Pending required checks, `not_ready_yet`, and any structured CI state other than `ci_absent_required` do not escalate. `packages/core/src/pr-merge-readiness/ci-gate.ts` 398-412 sets `ci_failures` even when absent contexts are also listed. `ci-gate.ts` 365-384 sets `ci_never_scheduled` when no workflow runs exist and the required-context list is empty. `monitor.ts` 231-248 then 250-254 waits until the cap and returns cap-reached. The default cap is 60 minutes (`monitor.ts` 170). The absent grace is one poll (`packages/core/src/pr-monitor/constants.ts` 13) and the first sleep is 60 seconds (`constants.ts` 16-19).

## In plain English

Problem: when a PR conflicts with its base branch, GitHub does not run the PR's CI, so the required checks never appear. The merge command waited, saw the checks missing, and reported `absent-required`. Workers read that as a CI problem and waited or escalated, while the real fix was to merge or rebase the base branch.

Accepted solution: when the monitor ends with `absent-required` or `cap-reached`, the merge command reads the PR once from GitHub. If GitHub says the PR's merge state is `dirty`, the command reports a new outcome, `base-conflict`, with exit 1 as before. Its error names the base branch and the fix: merge or rebase the base branch into the PR branch, resolve the conflicts, push, and run the command again. It says that required checks do not run on a conflicted PR only when the replaced result was `absent-required`. If the read fails, or GitHub gives any other state, the command reports exactly what it reports today. The read happens before any merge-queue enqueue, so a conflicted PR is never queued.

Limits accepted: reports that the command returns before the monitor (a review finding, a red master gate) keep their place; the next run after that fix reports the conflict. There is no check before the monitor starts. The merge-queue `--resume` / `--wait` path is unchanged. The design adds one read on two failing outcomes, one outcome name and one error text, and no new gate, refusal, flag, exit code or stored state. The design was checked by reading the source at the pinned commit; no code was run. No leftover next-build.

## Problem

When a PR conflicts with its base branch, `pr:wait-mergeable-and-merge` reports `absent-required` (TIMEOUT-OR-ESCALATION), not a conflict. GitHub does not run `pull_request` CI on a conflicted PR, so the required checks never appear. The worker reads this as a CI problem and waits or escalates. The merge queue says `removed` / `merge_conflict` only after a full cycle.

## Evidence

- `packages/core/src/pr-wait-mergeable/classify.ts` (origin/master `7aef28cb5`): monitor exit 4, or `monitor_result: ABSENT-REQUIRED`, maps to outcome `absent-required`. No branch reads `mergeable_state`.
- `packages/core/src/pr-monitor/monitor.ts`: `mergeable_state` is read only by `mergeStateFromPayload` for the per-poll heartbeat line. It does not change the result.
- `packages/core/src/pr-monitor/absent-required.ts`: `readAbsentRequiredContexts` decides from CI data only.
- Seen on 2026-11-16 after the v0.129.11 release commit: #6451 and #6456 (#6409 completion), #6447 and #6450 (#6336 completion), and #6452. Each one was reported as `absent-required` while the real cause was a conflict with master (reported by a worker, not re-read).

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a PR whose `mergeable_state` is `dirty`, when `pr:wait-mergeable-and-merge` runs, then it reports a conflict outcome that says the PR conflicts with its base and names the fix (merge or rebase the base branch).
- Given a PR whose `mergeable_state` is `dirty`, when its required checks are absent, then the verb does not report `absent-required`.
- Given a PR with no conflict and missing required checks, when the verb runs, then it still reports `absent-required` as today.

The outcomes the verb returns before the monitor (preflight refusals, `semantic-green-blocked` and its named outcomes, `new-p0-p1`) are unchanged.

Reader. One new reader in `packages/core/src/pr-wait-mergeable/` takes `mergeable_state` and `base.ref` from that one response. It is injectable through one new option on `WaitMergeableOptions`. Under the existing test-harness convention (`skipHumanMergeGate` or `VITEST`, no injected function) the read is skipped, as for `watchFn` and `mergeQueueDetectFn`.

Fallback. When the read fails, cannot be parsed, or gives any state other than `dirty` (including `unknown`, null, `blocked`, `behind` and `unstable`, whatever `mergeable` says), the verb reports today's outcome, exit code and error text unchanged.

Unchanged. No new exit code, flag, gate, refusal or stored state. The printed result label for exit 1 stays `TIMEOUT-OR-ESCALATION`; `outcome` and `error` carry the conflict. The merge-queue `--resume` / `--wait` path is not changed.

Given a monitor result `absent-required` and a read with `mergeable_state` `blocked`, when the verb runs, then the outcome is `absent-required` and the error text is the same as today.
Given a monitor result `absent-required` and a read that fails, or gives `unknown` or null, when the verb runs, then the outcome is `absent-required` and the error text is the same as today.
Given a read with `mergeable_state` `dirty` and no `base.ref`, when the verb reports `base-conflict`, then the error says "its base branch" and still names the fix.
Given a clean monitor result, when the verb runs, then the conflict read is not made.
Given a SHA-matched `new-p0-p1` probe before the monitor, when the verb runs, then the outcome is `new-p0-p1` and the conflict read is not made.
Given merge-queue mode, a monitor result `absent-required` and a `dirty` read, when the verb runs, then the outcome is `base-conflict` and the PR is not enqueued.
Given `--json` and a `base-conflict` result, then standard output is one JSON document with `outcome` `base-conflict` and the error text.
